Bullock
BOOL-'k
n. (rendering Hebrew par and b'n-bāqār)
From Old English bulluc, a diminutive of bull — a young bull. The Hebrew par denotes a young bull in its prime, and the fuller expression par ben-bāqār, a bullock the son of the herd, marks it as the most valuable single animal a man could bring. That value is the point: the bullock is the offering prescribed where the guilt is heaviest.

Biblical Definition

The bullock is the costliest of the ordinary sacrifices, and the law assigns it precisely where sin does the most damage. When the anointed priest sins, the offering required is not a lamb or a pigeon but the best of the herd: “If the priest that is anointed do sin according to the sin of the people; then let him bring for his sin, which he hath sinned, a young bullock without blemish unto the LORD for a sin offering” (Lev 4:3). The greater the office, the greater the reparation — because a priest's sin corrupts the very channel through which the people approach God. Yet Scripture never lets the ritual stand alone, and the prophets attack the assumption that God is supplied by the offering: “To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the LORD: I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks” (Isa 1:11). The psalmist states the ranking that governs the whole system: “This also shall please the LORD better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs” (Psa 69:31) — thanksgiving from a right heart outweighing the largest animal in the yard. And yet the sacrifices are not thereby abolished but reordered, for the same psalter promises that when the heart is right the altar will be used properly again: then shall they offer bullocks upon thine altar (Psa 51:19). Hebrews gives the reason the whole arrangement was provisional: if the blood of bulls and of goats sanctified to the purifying of the flesh (Heb 9:13), how much more the blood of Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

A young bull; in the Levitical law the costliest of the ordinary sacrifices, required for the sin of the anointed priest and of the whole congregation, and the type whose insufficiency Hebrews sets against the blood of Christ.

BULLOCK, n. 1. An ox, or castrated bull; in the Scriptures, a young bull.

2. In the Levitical law, the chief of the offerings, appointed for the sin of the priest and of the whole congregation. Levit. 4.

3. The most costly of the beasts of the herd; whence the offering of bullocks denotes the fullest measure of sacrifice.

4. In the Hebrew, par, a young bull in his strength; also a bullock the son of the herd.

5. In Scripture, I delight not in the blood of bullocks. Isaiah 1. The blood of bulls and of goats. Heb. 9.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 4:3 — "If the priest that is anointed do sin according to the sin of the people; then let him bring for his sin, which he hath sinned, a young bullock without blemish unto the LORD for a sin offering."

Isaiah 1:11 — "To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the LORD: I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats."

Psalm 69:31 — "This also shall please the LORD better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs."

Hebrews 9:13 — "For if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh:"

Modern Corruption

The sacrificial system is read either as evidence that Israel's God required appeasement like the pagan deities, or as a merely symbolic ritual with no real substitution — both of which empty the doctrine of penal substitution the bullock was given to teach.

expand to see more

The first corruption presents the Levitical offerings as appeasement of an angry deity, indistinguishable in kind from the sacrifices of Canaan, and then treats the New Testament's doctrine of the cross as the same primitive idea carried forward. The difference is fundamental and the texts insist on it. The pagan sacrifice is offered to a god by men seeking to change his disposition; the Levitical sacrifice is appointed by the LORD Himself, who declares in advance that He has given the blood upon the altar to make atonement. The initiative, the prescription, and the provision are all God's. That is why Isaiah can have God say He is full of the burnt offerings of rams (Isa 1:11) — He is not fed by them, was never fed by them, and never claimed to be. The offering was pedagogy in blood: a demonstration that sin costs a life.

The opposite corruption drains the offerings of any real substitution and makes them merely expressive — symbols of devotion, gifts of gratitude, with no transfer of guilt. The ritual itself forbids the reading. The offerer lays his hand on the head of the bullock, and the identification is explicit; the animal dies in his place; the blood is applied. Hebrews argues from the reality of that transaction, not against it, and its whole case is how much more: if the blood of bulls sanctified to the purifying of the flesh (Heb 9:13), how much more shall the blood of Christ purge your conscience. The principle to recover is that the bullock was a real substitute and an insufficient one, and that its insufficiency is precisely what taught Israel to look for a better sacrifice — offered once, by a Priest who did not first need to bring a bullock for Himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew par is a young bull in its prime; b'n-bāqār is a bullock the son of the herd, marking its pedigree and value; 'egel is a calf. The sin offering of the priest and of the congregation alike required the bullock.

expand to see more

Hebrew par (H6499) — a young bull or bullock; the chief animal of the sin offering and of the great burnt offerings.

Hebrew par ben-bāqār — a bullock the son of the herd; the full designation in Lev 4:3, marking the animal's value and pedigree.

Hebrew 'egel (H5695) — a calf; the animal of the golden calf and of the fatted calf, distinguished from the full-grown par.

Hebrew s'mīkâh — the laying on of the offerer's hand upon the head of the victim (Lev 4:4), the act of identification and transfer.

Greek tauros (G5022) — a bull or ox; the blood of bulls and of goats (Heb 9:13), which cannot take away sins.

Usage

"Of the priest's sin offering: let him bring... a young bullock without blemish unto the LORD for a sin offering (Lev 4:3)."

"Of the prophetic rebuke of mere ritual: I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats (Isa 1:11)."

"Of thanksgiving ranked above the offering: this also shall please the LORD better than an ox or bullock (Psa 69:31)."
